1:
The rule about blemished victims is short, and they enlarge it alike. Henry gives the principle — God is the best of beings, and whatever he is served with ought to be the best in its kind — and notes that the second word might better be rendered any evil matter or thing, covering sickness not discernible at first view. Clarke makes it a test anyone can apply: God must not have offered to him what you would not use yourself. Gill and Henry make the victim a type of the Lamb without blemish, and Clarke extends it to the worshipper, to the uprightness of heart God requires. Wesley notes that bullock and sheep stand for the greater and smaller sacrifices, two kinds standing for all.

Ellicott alone asks why the precept is here at all, the law of the purity of victims being given in full elsewhere. His answer is that one principle unites the apparently unrelated topics of these chapters — the holy days, the administration of justice, the absence of groves and images, the perfection of sacrifices — the holiness of the God of Israel necessitating them all. He and Henry converge from different directions on the same observation: the one period when imperfect creatures were complained of on any scale was when the blind and the lame were brought for sacrifice, after the captivity had cured the nation of idolatry.

On the idolater's death Calvin is concerned with what the law equates. The same punishment is decreed here as against apostates, so that corrupting God's worship by gross superstition is reckoned no less weighty than abandoning religion altogether. He fixes on the phrase transgressing his covenant: the thief, the fornicator and the drunkard transgress the Law but are not in this category, because what is punished here is not simple impiety but the perfidy of forsaking true religion after having devoted oneself to God. Wesley reaches the same conclusion by another road, calling idolatry a breach of faith given to God and a dissolution of a matrimonial covenant. Henry sharpens the parallel with the preceding chapter: it was already capital to seduce others to idolatry, and here it is made no less a crime to be seduced — if the blind mislead the blind, both fall into the ditch; and yet the law which works death proved ineffectual.

Calvin and Keil both mark the checks. Calvin lists the tokens of severity — a woman to die as well as a man, the whole people joining in the stoning, the evil removed from the midst of the land — and against them the tokens of moderation: diligent inquiry made, no sentence pronounced unless the matter is fully proved, and one man's accusation unable to convict. God would not have judges shed blood inconsiderately under pretext of zeal. Keil states the same as procedure: the facts carefully inquired into, death only on the testimony of two or three and never of one, the witnesses' own hands first upon the condemned, and the execution at the gate of the town where the crime was committed. Calvin adds that the repetition of that man or that woman is deliberate, since the weakness of the sex might have been thought to extenuate the guilt and here may not.

The idolatry named draws two comments. Henry observes that the form specified is the most ancient and plausible, the worship of sun and moon and stars — and if that was so detestable, how much more the worship of stocks and stones; and that if nothing more could be said against it than that God had not commanded it, that alone had been enough. Wesley adds a grammatical note: I have not commanded means I have forbidden, such negative expressions being emphatical. Gill reports the Targum's expansion, that the offender went after the evil imagination.
4:
Calvin reads the requirement of diligent inquiry as cutting both ways, and that is the freshest thing here. Judges are not only restrained from precipitate condemnation; they are stimulated to beware of passing over in idleness anything that needed to be known. They often fail in their duty, he says, because they wilfully connive at guilt, so that what would be manifest if they took the pains does not come to light — God would have them neither slumber nor ignore sinister reports, so that no crime may remain unpunished. Clarke reads the same verse as a sequence of filters: told privately by some confidential person, then found notorious and publicly scandalous, then examined as to the persons reporting and the circumstances, then found not to rest on rumour or malice, and at last substantiated by the fullest evidence — all necessary, since the charge affected a man's life. Gill agrees that such a report was not to be neglected though not to be concluded on by hearsay, and gives the Targum's gloss that the witnesses were to be well questioned as to proof, persons, time, place and manner.

Why the number of witnesses is two or three, and not one and not more, gets a practical answer. Calvin observes that the severity with which God exacts punishment for murder shows how highly he rates human life, and that this rule shows equal care for innocent blood, nothing being more dangerous than to expose a man's life to the tongue of a single individual — but he balances it with a consideration none of the others raise: if two or three would not suffice, there would be no end to litigation. Clarke gives the simple ground that one witness might be deceived or prejudiced or malicious. Wesley adds the rabbinic exclusions, that the testimony of children, women, servants, familiar friends or enemies, and persons of dissolute life or evil fame was rejected. Gill reports two further rabbinic refinements — that a third witness turns the scale where two contradict two, and that two wise men might serve where three others were needed — and one about form: because the text says at the mouth of the witnesses, testimony was held to be necessarily spoken, at their mouth and not from their handwriting.

That the witnesses must throw the first stones is explained the same way by three of them and elaborated by one. Gill says it was a further confirmation of their testimony, since to begin the stoning readily would show both zeal for the honour of God and an unconsciousness of guilt in what they had sworn. Wesley says it was for the caution of witnesses, that if they had accused falsely through malice or wrath they might now be afraid to imbrue their hands in innocent blood. Calvin puts the psychology most sharply: the office is laid on the witnesses because the tongue of many is too hasty, so that they do not hesitate to stab people verbally when they would not dare to lay a finger on them, and it is therefore an excellent remedy against light accusations to admit no testimony from anyone whose hand is not prepared to execute the sentence. He adds two observations of his own. The ancient people employed no public executioners, so that there might be more solemnity and reverence in punishment. And stoning was probably chosen because it required many hands — other capital punishments existed, since a hanged body was to be taken down before sunset — but where the land was purged as by a propitiation the whole people cast at once, both to prove their indignation and because stoning one after another would have made the death lingering and cruel.
8:
The three pairs of terms are unpacked twice. Keil renders the opening as a matter too marvellous for judgment, meaning too difficult to decide, and takes the pairs to mean it is unclear by what provision a fatal blow, a civil dispute or a bodily injury is to be settled; he also insists on who is addressed. Israel is spoken to as a nation, but the words go neither to the local courts first and the litigants last, nor to the parties, but to those charged with administering justice. Henry translates the same pairs into the vocabulary of English law: blood and blood is the blood that cried against the blood demanded, where it was doubtful whether the killing was wilful or casual; plea and plea is the declaration of plaintiff against defendant; stroke and stroke is an action of assault and battery. He adds the essential point that the difficulty need not be evidential — though the evidence were plain, doubts might arise about the sense of the law and its application — so that the inferior court must, in the language of his own courts, find a special verdict and take time to advise. Wesley sorts the same pairs as capital, civil and criminal causes, a matter becoming controversial when the magistrates were divided.

Who the appeal lies to is disputed, and the dispute is about the words the judge. Wesley takes him to be probably the high priest, named separately because among the priests he especially was to be consulted. Calvin refutes that: the opinion is easily answered, since the text distinctly enumerates the priests, the Levites and the judge. He allows the singular may stand for a plurality, and appeals to Jehoshaphat's appointment of Levites and priests to preside at Jerusalem, where the high priest was over matters of the Lord and the king's governor over civil causes. Gill settles on a third: since no single ruler such as Othniel or Gideon was always in being, he prefers the president of the great sanhedrin.

What the priests are for, in Calvin's account, is larger than this passage. Their principal office is described under a single head, that they should declare what is right in doubtful matters out of the Law of God; and though the text seems to refer only to civil controversies, it appoints them interpreters of its doctrine as well. His argument is from the greater to the less: if their sentence must be submitted to where a man's life is at stake, all exception is removed with respect to God's worship. He concedes that the priests are not the sole judges, but holds the dignity of the priesthood especially exalted. Clarke gives the practical reason in one line: the priests and Levites, being lawyers by birth and continual practice, were reasonably considered best qualified to decide difficult points.

How far the decision binds is the sharpest division here, and a straight contradiction. Gill lays down a limit: the court was not to make any new law but to teach the law of God, and so far as their sense of things agreed with it they were to be regarded. Wesley denies the limit — the judge is confined to his rule in giving sentence, but it is fit that people be bound simply to acquiesce in the sentence of their last and highest judge, or else there would be no end of strife. Calvin here sides with Wesley, requiring acquiescence even on the most disagreeable points — though he qualifies it sharply a verse later. Keil states the sanction without softening it: none was to resist in pride, resistance to the priest being dissatisfaction with his interpretation and resistance to the judge discontent with the sentence founded on it, such conduct being punished with death as rebellion against God, in whose name the right had been spoken.
12:
Having just demanded acquiescence in the priests' sentence, Calvin now takes much of it back, and the two passages must be read together. The priests were not armed with tyrannical authority, so that it should be sinful to reject whatever they decreed of their own fancy: God did not dethrone himself when he appointed them, nor bind men's consciences to obey their ordinances without distinction, but only put reins on those who think nothing of undervaluing the government of the Church. Foul disorder would follow if men might reject whatever the rulers appointed, and it would be ridiculous to call persons to govern and accord them no dignity; but reverence is due to all lawful commands, and God has never exalted a mortal so high as to abdicate his own rights — indeed, it has often been necessary boldly to reject what the priests commanded. Clarke states the ground of the penalty more narrowly: the man who refused the final determination was in rebellion against the highest authority, and the public could have no pledge for his conduct. Calvin adds that the publicity is the point, impunity baiting sin.

Whether the law about a king approves of kings gets four answers, none a simple yes. Henry says a king is neither promised as a mercy nor commanded as a duty but permitted, and that provided the ends of government were answered they were not tied to any one form; the motive was irregular, a wish to be like the nations from which God had distinguished them, but God would indulge it because he meant to make the regal government typical of the kingdom of the Messiah. Keil puts it structurally: an earthly kingdom was not opposed to the rule of Jehovah provided the king was the man Jehovah chose, and the appointment is not commanded as the institution of judges was, since Israel could exist under God's government without a king. Gill notes that the Jews took the verse for a command, and denies it. Wesley goes furthest: God only foresees and foretells what they would do without approving it, and when they did it for this very reason he declared his utter dislike.

Calvin's objection is historical rather than constitutional. Under the judges the very difference of their government separated the Jews from the nations round about, all of whom had kings; once they chose kings they were so mixed with the Gentiles that it became easy to fall into other corruptions, the similarity of governments uniting them more closely. That is why the text says pointedly like as all the nations that are about thee. He adds that the splendour of the royal name might make them forget that God retained the sovereignty.

On the two restrictions they agree. That the choice is God's and not the people's, Calvin reads as a rebuke of their audacity in demanding a king by hasty impulse; Henry gives the principle that kings are God's vicegerents and it is fit he should choose them; Wesley notes that God reserved the nomination both of the family and of the person; Gill observes that when in later times they appointed kings without consulting him, it is complained of. That the king must be a brother, Calvin explains by the risk of apostasy, a foreigner forcing his native gods on them and persecuting true religion by the royal power. Wesley adds that a brother was likeliest to maintain religion and rule with gentleness, and would be a fit type of Christ, who was to be one of their brethren. Clarke alone carries the clause into the Gospels: it was on the ground of this command that the question about tribute to Caesar was put, they being then under a foreign power, so that an affirmative answer would have condemned him by this law and a negative would have been reported to Caesar.
16:
The horses are forbidden for opposite reasons, pointing in opposite geographical directions. Clarke and Wesley take the danger to be traffic with Egypt, which furnished Canaan with horses: Clarke fears the commerce would lead to idolatry, that reliance on cavalry would displace trust in God, and that extending dominion by cavalry would scatter Israel among the nations and destroy the distinctness on which the Messianic prophecies depended. Wesley allows horses for the king's own use but not for officers and guard. Calvin construes the doubled clause differently. Taking the particle as for the sake of, he reads the prohibition as condemning an immoderate stud for what it would lead to — a king with many horses being tempted to march an army into Egypt. The fear is invasion, not import. He prefaces it with a principle: royal power must be kept within legal bounds lest it act like a runaway horse, the desires of kings being insatiable. Gill keeps to the domestic reason, that a standing force would let the king tyrannise over his subjects.

On the wives Calvin makes an argument from the law's very restriction. Polygamy then prevailed so generally that the humblest violated the marriage vow with impunity, and kings needed closer restraint lest their example countenance incontinency — which refutes those who conclude that what was forbidden to kings was thereby permitted to private men. He adds the expense, such being the ambition of women that each would have desired royal treatment. Where the others make the turning away of the heart the reason for the prohibition, Calvin takes it separately, as a warning that the splendour of the dignity may unsettle the judgment, nothing being harder than for a man in power to remain temperate. Gill and Clarke instance Solomon, Clarke adding that many wives meant foreign alliances and the idolatry that came with them. On the treasure Calvin is hardest: it is forbidden because it cannot be heaped up without rapine and violent exactions.

What the king had to write out is disputed by all who touch it. Gill reports that the versions take it for Deuteronomy and the Jewish writers for the whole Pentateuch, thinking the latter perhaps too much and the restriction to this law about kings too little. Calvin rejects the narrow reading: the whole sum of doctrine is meant, what is delivered in Exodus and Leviticus as well as here. Clarke and Ellicott both observe that the phrase is the source of the book's Greek and modern name; Ellicott adds that the Hebrew word became the name of the Talmud's text, whose idea is to repeat the law — a peculiar repetition, dealing in minutiae and leaving the weightier matters out.

The manner of copying draws a point about textual transmission and one about kings. Wesley says the king wrote it with his own hand, from the original kept by the priests; Clarke makes that original the standard from which every copy was taken and against which each was compared, and thinks the priests probably revised every transcript to keep errors from creeping into the sacred text. Calvin has the priests present the book in a solemn ceremony, as though God deposited a treasure with the king — and gives the reason for the lifelong reading with some bitterness: kings are usually supplied with books out of ostentation, and having tasted them grow tired and cease to read. Ellicott finds traces of the practice at the coronation of Joash and in the reading to Josiah of the book found in the temple, remarking that it is singular we hear nothing of it in connection with David or Solomon. He ends on the true king of Israel, whose mission was to fulfil the law and the prophets — Lo, I come; in the volume of the book it is written of me.
19:
Why the king had to copy the law out himself is answered by Clarke in constitutional terms. It was the surest way of bringing him to an acquaintance with the divine law, and it was necessary because these laws were permanent and no Israelitish king could make a new one, the kings of this people being always considered mere vicegerents of Jehovah. Gill takes the phrase it shall be with him literally — the book was to go wherever he went, at home or abroad, whether he sat on his throne or lay down, except in places where it was not proper to read; and the reading was to be daily meditation. Wesley turns the same clause on the reader: it is not enough to have Bibles, but we must use them, and use them daily, our souls needing constant meals of that manna, which if well digested will afford them true nourishment and strength.

What the reading was to prevent is agreed in substance and differently grounded. Gill says the heart was not to be lifted up on account of the office, since the king was himself subject to the law of God and accountable to him for all his actions, and that ruling well according to those laws was the way to rule long. Wesley presses the psychology: the scriptures diligently read are a powerful means of keeping a king humble, because they show him that though a king he is subject to a higher monarch, to whom he must give account of all his administrations and from whom he must receive a sentence agreeable to their quality — which is enough, he says, to abate the pride of the haughtiest person in the world.

The promise about his children divides them three ways, and the question is whether the crown was hereditary. Clarke thinks it was designed to be, and defends the arrangement on general grounds outside the text altogether: long experience has proved to almost all the nations of the world that hereditary succession in regal government is on the whole the safest and best calculated to secure the public tranquillity. Gill, following a rabbinic comment, makes it elective but with a standing preference — if the king's son was fit for the kingdom he was to be preferred before any other man, so that the crown continued in the same family provided they walked in the ways of the Lord. Ellicott denies the inference in the form Clarke gives it: the verse shows that the kingdom would be hereditary only so far as Jehovah willed it to be so. He then adds an observation that is really an argument about the book itself. No dynasty except David's ever continued for more than five generations, and only two for more than two, while David's was perpetual by promise — a striking fact which, he says, could hardly have escaped notice if it had been known to the writer of this book.
